memorials.name: Chris Williams
memorials.note: The author of "Coldblooded" Kain Threat and a former PWW executive and Television Champion who died in an automobile accident. After his death, the PWW Chris Williams Television Championship was named in his honor. For at least eight years thereafter, the wider e-fedding community and "an ever increasing circle of friends" gathered together to pay respect to his memory with an independent tournament: the Chris Williams Memorial Cup.

memorials.name: Joe Smallze
memorials.note: He e-wrestled for roughly six years, on and off, starting in the NAWA and ending in Furiously Addictive Wrestling (FAW), a PTC member fed — in the period record's own words, "one of the greatest competitors to ever roleplay." He died of a methadone overdose in April 2002 — the fed's own announcement places it early Tuesday, 23 Apr 2002; the tribute that followed says he fell asleep on the 21st and passed on the 22nd. He brought his own cousin into e-fedding; that cousin, the handler of FAW's own Hardcore Hoefel, wrote the tribute that named them both. FAW retired its own new Television Championship unfilled in his name rather than crown it on anyone else, and its roster paid tribute to him on Distortion, the show he never got to wrestle again.

memorials.name: Tim Fitzgerald
memorials.note: The creator of WrestleCrazy Entertainment and Mayhem Wrestling Entertainment, and the reason — in his own community's words — that a whole family of federations existed at all: "without Tim Fitzgerald, there would have been NO WcE, WWA, eWa, SWA, WHQ, or MWE." He appeared on his own shows as Rocky Stevens and wrestled in WHQ and, in 2007, in MWE as John Austin, but the work he was loved for happened behind the scenes: welcoming newcomers other boards had chased off, coaching writers one at a time, and posting shows week after week. He died on 20 March 2008, the day MWE closed its doors. His roster rebuilt the company in his honor and marked the first anniversary with a memorial supershow — "TF" armbands in the ring, his portrait hung beside the champions he made, an annual award in his name for the craft he loved best — and a roleplay titled In Tim We Trust, the board’s own pick for roleplay of the year in 2009.

memorials.name: Ed Wilson
memorials.note: The owner of the Cyber Wrestling League — in his own community's words, "a league that visually changed fantasy wrestling." A husband as well as a doctor, he was killed in the first week of May 2001, struck by a car as he left the hospital where he worked. The news reached the hobby through fantasywrestling.com's own front page, written out of fiction by that hub's own operator — one portal stopping its presses to mourn the founder of another, and a peer hub's FAQ had already counted his league's initials among the handful every newcomer was told were too well known to reuse.

memorials.name: Chad Dupree
memorials.commemorated_by: the museum, and the Chad Dupree Memorial Cup — EUWC's own annual tournament, renewed by the community year after year
memorials.note: A mainstay on the FW circuit, he wrote as "Mr. Main Event" Rob Sampson, ran the EUWC and co-owned GXW. In a fellow handler's own words, Chad Dupree was "a phenomenal roleplayer, a dedicated federation owner, and a good friend," one who "would stick with me and give me advice when it seemed as though nobody... was on my side." After his death, EUWC named its annual tournament the Chad Dupree Memorial Cup; by 2006, the Cup was being staged across the wider circuit. Years after he died, handlers were still posting on his birthday to raise a toast in his honor.

memorials.name: Ron Olson
memorials.commemorated_by: the museum, on a fellow participant's account
memorials.note: He wrote The Rock, a World Heavyweight title contender in the Almost Illegal Wrestling League, in the years when a league lived on an Angelfire page and a weekly card. A fellow handler remembered him as an average New Englander who grew up in Tewksbury, Massachusetts, played high-school sports and college baseball, and was killed in a car crash in 2004 at twenty-two.

memorials.name: Andy Doran
memorials.note: An English teacher and football coach in Allentown, Pennsylvania, whose obituary noted that he "enjoyed a wrestling based creative writing circle." He wrote as Marcus Broussard and "Cool Hand" Luke Kinsey, served on EMWC's staff until its close in 2003, and was named co-winner of Best Handler in the newsgroup's 2004 year-end awards. He was so beloved within the community that his death led JTF Squaretable to cancel its 2015 Hall of Fame awards, the first break in nearly a decade. When the awards returned in 2017, they came with a new wing of the Hall of Fame honoring out-of-character accomplishments: the Andy Doran Wing.

memorials.name: Paul Scanlan
memorials.commemorated_by: the museum, and a fellow writer's tribute on PRIME's ReVolution 244, 14 April 2011
memorials.note: Of Brentwood, Essex, he wrote Paul Cain and Damien Kahn through NWC: Atlantic, NWC: South, PRIME, CCW and Lone Star Wrestling, where Paul Cain held the NWC: Atlantic Heavyweight and CCW World Heavyweight titles. Paul Cain also wrestled for Ultimate Championship Wrestling, NeWA and Simcoe County Championship Wrestling. A fellow writer remembered him as one of the few who befriended a newcomer, and as "a champion in life." He died on 9 April 2011. Five days later PRIME's ReVolution 244 paid him tribute and dedicated an Intense Championship to his name, the one PRIME title his writing had never won.

memorials.name: Daniel Quirk
memorials.note: He ran the EWF in the late 1990s until it became part of CWF-Pro, after which he wrote as the Punisher. CWF-Pro inducted him into its Hall of Fame in 2001. He became a professional wrestler in 2002 and worked independent wrestling shows across the Northeast as Spider. He died after an accident at an Ultimate Championship Wrestling event in Massachusetts in 2005, aged 22. On June 11, 2005, Connecticut Championship Wrestling dedicated its WrestleJam 2 supercard to Quirk's memory.

memorials.name: Patrick Little
memorials.note: He created ICW, Internet Championship Wrestling, in June 1998, running it as Big Dawg and wrestling as Strider, its World Champion. As ICW went under he wrestled for GCW as Titan and Strider, later serving as its Commissioner. He died on 31 December 1999, a day after an accident. GCW dedicated Survivor Match '00 to him and inducted him into its Hall of Fame in 2001. The man who built GCW wrote that "without him, there would be no us," and signed his posts "RIPPL": Rest In Peace Patrick Little.

memorials.name: Frank A. Marano Jr.
memorials.commemorated_by: the museum; SJPW's Frank A. Marano Jr. Memorial Tag Team Tournament, its pay-per-view of 16–18 January 1998; and the Frank A. Marano Jr. Memorial Cup, a tag team tournament first held in 1993 and renewed in 1996 and from 2005
memorials.note: He founded the Universal Wrestling Alliance, a play-by-mail league of the 1980s, from the years before the internet when wrestling shows reached their players as printed newsletters. A friend remembered it as "the cream of the crop", and remembered him running eight regional UWAs at once, from Canada to Japan, through Hodgkin's disease and a stroke. The cancer took his life in 1993. SJPW, whose characters traced their careers to his UWA, bade him "Good night, Frank. We'll always remember you" in August 1997 and staged the Frank A. Marano Jr. Memorial Tag Team Tournament that winter and the next. The Frank A. Marano Jr. Memorial Cup, first held in 1993, was still being contested in 2010.
